newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutor urges Kevorkian jury to ignore emotions.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor urges Kevorkian jury to ignore emotions.

text.p: The county prosecutor urged jurors in his opening statement on Wednesday to follow the law and not be swayed by emotion in deciding the fate of Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the advocate of assisted suicide.

Kevorkian's attorney Geoffrey Fieger fired back by accusing prosecutor Raymond Voet of being on a "witch hunt" and harassing family members of a woman whom Kevorkian allegedly helped to kill herself last August.
The 69-year-old retired pathologist is charged with four felonies in connection with the Aug. 30 death of Loretta Peabody, 54, who had multiple sclerosis.
In a subdued opening statement, Voet told the jurors in the conservative western Michigan town of Ionia they were not in court for a town hall meeting on assisted suicide.
"If you base your decision upon sympathy and prejudice, when this case is over, then you violated your oath," he said.
Voet also warned jurors that members of Peabody's family, who have been given immunity from prosecution in the case, might not be happy with his decision to prosecute Kevorkian.
"I'm not asking you to judge the Loretta Peabody family, I'm not asking you to judge Loretta Peabody," he said. "I'm asking you to judge Jack Kevorkian."

Standing in front of an enlarged photograph of a smiling Loretta Peabody, Fieger attacked prosecutors for allegedly harassing the Peabody family by investigating the remarriage of Loretta Peabody's former husband Joesph six months after she died.
"This is a real witch hunt. What's sad about this case is the torture of this family," he said.
Lowering his voice, Fieger appealed to the jury to draw on its sense of civic duty to protect the Peabodys.
"Your're the jury. You're the conscience of this community. You are their neighbours. You are the people. And they need your help -- now. They need you to say never, ever again," he said.
Fieger also attacked the unwritten "common law" that the Michigan Supreme Court in a 1994 decision ruled banned assisted suicide.

Earlier, Voet dropped his objections to Kevorkian's request to stay away from the trial. Kevorkian was acquitted in three trials in the Detroit area between 1994 and 1996. If convicted of assisting suicide, he could face up to five years in prison and a fine of $10,000.
